title: Brute Force Login Attacks
description: Stop wp-login.php brute force attacks, reduce server load, and harden authentication without locking out legitimate users.

steps.title: Confirm Brute Force Attack
steps.instructions: Check server logs for repeated POST requests to wp-login.php or xmlrpc.php. Note spike in failed login attempts and server CPU from security plugin logs.

steps.title: Enable Login Rate Limiting
steps.instructions: Configure Wordfence, Solid Security, or Limit Login Attempts Reloaded. Set lockout threshold (e.g. 3 failures, 20-minute lockout) and whitelist agency IPs.

steps.title: Enforce Two-Factor Authentication
steps.instructions: Require 2FA for all administrator accounts. Even if passwords are guessed, 2FA blocks unauthorized access.

steps.title: Change Default Login URL (Optional)
steps.instructions: Use WPS Hide Login or server rules to move wp-login.php to a custom slug. This reduces automated bot traffic but is not a substitute for strong auth.

steps.title: Disable or Restrict XML-RPC
steps.instructions: Brute force often targets xmlrpc.php. Disable if Jetpack/mobile apps do not need it. Block via .htaccess or security plugin.

steps.title: Enable CDN or WAF Bot Protection
steps.instructions: Cloudflare Bot Fight Mode, Sucuri WAF, or host-level WAF can block attack traffic before it hits PHP. Enable challenge rules for wp-login.php.

steps.title: Audit Usernames and Passwords
steps.instructions: Remove 'admin' username. Force password reset for weak passwords. Disable unused accounts and application passwords.

steps.title: Monitor Attack Volume Post-Fix
steps.instructions: Confirm failed login rate drops and server load normalizes. Ensure agency and client staff can still log in from all locations.
